justice: Pedestrian space is unevenly distributed: the left side has a narrow raised walkway while the right side is largely unpaved dirt and rubble, giving different users very unequal street access conditions.
There is no visible dedicated bicycle lane, so cyclists and electric two-wheelers must mix with cars in the main carriageway rather than receiving comparable space allocation.
Accessibility is limited because no marked curb ramps, tactile paving, or protected crossings are visible, and the roadside guardrail on the left may constrain entry and exit to the walkway.
safety: Cars, scooters, and motorcycles are sharing the same undivided roadway, increasing conflict risk between different traffic speeds and vehicle types.
A child is standing near the rough dirt shoulder on the right side without a sidewalk or protective barrier, indicating weak pedestrian protection from moving vehicles.
The right roadside contains rubble, uneven ground, utility poles, and a large overhead pipeline close to the travel edge, creating roadside hazards and reducing recovery space.
livability: Small shops and low-rise buildings on the left suggest some everyday service presence and local activity, which supports basic neighborhood function.
However, the industrial character created by the large overhead pipe, power infrastructure, and vacant rubble-strewn edge weakens the sense of a pleasant community street.
The lack of visible seating, public gathering space, or quality pedestrian frontage reduces the street's usefulness as a social and everyday public environment.
sustainability: A few mature street trees on the left provide some ecological value and shade, but greenery is concentrated on one side and overall coverage is limited.
No visible protected cycling facilities, bus stop infrastructure, or high-quality pedestrian facilities are present to strongly support low-carbon travel choices.
The unpaved shoulder, exposed soil, and construction debris on the right indicate weak green infrastructure and poor stormwater-sensitive or environmentally maintained streetscape design.
aesthetics: The large tree canopy on the left adds some visual softness and improves the streetscape more than the rest of the corridor.
Visual quality is reduced by the exposed overhead pipeline, dense utility structures and wires, and the rough industrial edge along the right side.
Construction debris, bare ground, and inconsistent roadside treatment create a cluttered and poorly maintained appearance.
comfort: Thermal comfort is mixed: the large trees on the left provide shade, but most of the roadway and the entire right side appear exposed to direct sun.
Physical comfort is low because pedestrians lack a continuous, smooth sidewalk network, and the right shoulder is rough, dusty, and uneven.
Psychological comfort is reduced by mixed traffic, narrow edge conditions, and the presence of industrial infrastructure and rubble close to where pedestrians might walk.
walkability: There is no clearly continuous sidewalk on both sides of the street; the left side is narrow and constrained, while the right side is essentially an unpaved shoulder.
No visible crosswalk markings, pedestrian refuge, or signalized pedestrian infrastructure are present, which weakens route continuity and crossing safety.
Mixed traffic with scooters, motorcycles, and cars on the same carriageway makes walking feel less secure and less attractive for everyday trips.
bikeability: There is no visible bike lane or protected cycling space, so cyclists must ride directly in mixed traffic with cars and scooters.
The roadway edge on the right is rough and debris-filled, leaving little forgiving space for cycling and making it harder to ride safely near the curb.
No bicycle parking, bike symbols, colored lane markings, or intersection treatments are visible to support convenient and legible bicycle use.
